summary: 25 years in the tech industry with experience in hardware (e.g., Dell), software, networks, and infrastructure; last 10 years focused on AI, quantum computing, and data center strategy; CTO-level role overseeing AI and quantum strategy in the data center sector; product development experience in energy optimization and orchestration platforms; lecturer on AI and data science at a major UK university. Believes the current demand for power and compute in data centers is unprecedented and will drive both opportunity and disruption for years to come. Sees significant value in niche third-party solutions like Emerald for accelerating time-to-power and optimizing energy, but doubts hyperscalers will build these capabilities in-house in the near term. Views the market opportunity as massive but multifaceted, with long-term upside for companies that can expand beyond their current niche.
takeaways: Speed to power (time to grid connection) is currently the most valuable factor for data centers, often outweighing cost considerations (Q3)

Emerald's value proposition lies in enabling flexible power loads and faster grid connections, which is especially relevant in markets with long interconnection queues (e.g., Northern Virginia, ERCOT, Ireland) (Q3)

There is a strong advantage for third-party vendors like Emerald to serve as intermediaries between utilities and data centers, providing standardized solutions that utilities can more easily integrate than bespoke hyperscaler solutions (Q3)

Partnerships with major hardware vendors (e.g., NVIDIA's Vera Rubin DSX reference design) could provide Emerald with a distribution advantage, but widespread deployment is constrained by engineering and retrofitting challenges (Q3)

The market for grid and energy optimization in data centers is extremely large (hundreds of billions of dollars in inefficiencies), but Emerald's current niche is much smaller; long-term growth depends on expanding their solution set and adapting to evolving industry needs (Q3)
